section-4: More poetic devices: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds ('the rain in Spain'); consonance repeats consonant sounds within or at the end of words; onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds ('buzz', 'hiss'); imagery appeals to the senses; a symbol is an object that stands for a wider idea (a rose for love); hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration; apostrophe directly addresses an absent person, object or idea ('O Death'); oxymoron joins contradictory words ('sweet sorrow'); and paradox is a statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth.

Example of allegory: John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress', where the journey of Christian represents the spiritual life of a believer. Example of allusion: calling someone 'a Good Samaritan' refers to the Bible. When answering, define the term and give a short example.
section-5: A ballad (folk ballad or literary ballad) usually has four-line stanzas (quatrains), a refrain, simple language, dialogue and a tragic or supernatural story, e.g. 'Sir Patrick Spens' and Keats's 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci'. An epic has a heroic central figure, a vast setting, supernatural elements and an elevated style, e.g. Homer's 'Iliad', Milton's 'Paradise Lost' and the 'Mahabharata'.

An elegy is a mournful poem for the dead, e.g. Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' and Milton's 'Lycidas' (a pastoral elegy). A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling; an ode is an elaborate lyric addressed to someone or something (Pindaric, Horatian and irregular odes); and a sonnet has fourteen lines, either Petrarchan (octave and sestet) or Shakespearean (three quatrains and a couplet).
section-6: Blank verse was introduced into English by the Earl of Surrey and used by Marlowe, Shakespeare and Milton. Iambic pentameter consists of five iambs (unstressed-stressed syllables) per line, e.g. 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'. Free verse was popularised by Walt Whitman and modern poets like T.S. Eliot.

Other structural terms: a heroic couplet is a pair of rhymed iambic pentameter lines (used by Pope and Dryden); a quatrain has four lines; a tercet three; a stanza is a group of lines forming a unit; metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables (iambic, trochaic, anapaestic, dactylic); and rhyme scheme is shown by letters such as abab.
section-7: The poem (1819) is a literary ballad in twelve quatrains. The first three stanzas are spoken by an unnamed questioner who meets a pale, lonely knight-at-arms 'alone and palely loitering' by a lake where 'the sedge has withered' and 'no birds sing'. The rest of the poem is the knight's reply: he met a beautiful 'faery's child' in the meads, made her garlands, set her on his horse, and she fed him 'roots of relish sweet, and honey wild, and manna-dew'. She took him to her 'elfin grot', where he fell asleep and dreamed of pale kings, princes and warriors who cried 'La Belle Dame sans Merci hath thee in thrall!'. He woke on the cold hill side.

Themes: the destructive power of love and beauty, illusion versus reality, enchantment and loss, and the Romantic interest in the supernatural and medieval. The circular structure (the last stanza echoes the first) and the shortened fourth line of each stanza create a haunting effect. The title, meaning 'The Beautiful Lady Without Mercy', comes from a medieval French poem by Alain Chartier.
section-8: Antithesis is the placing of contrasting ideas in balanced phrases ('To err is human, to forgive divine'). Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking or writing, using devices like rhetorical questions, repetition and parallelism. Satire uses humour, irony and ridicule to criticise human folly or vice; it may be Horatian (gentle) or Juvenalian (bitter).

Other prose terms include tone (the writer's attitude), style, irony, parody, anecdote and character sketch. Types of essays include periodical essays (Addison and Steele), personal essays (Charles Lamb), formal essays (Francis Bacon, the 'father of the English essay') and argumentative essays.
section-9: 'The Spectator Club' appeared in 'The Spectator' No. 2 (1711), a periodical run by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele. The club members are: Sir Roger de Coverley, a kind, slightly eccentric country gentleman representing the landed gentry; a member of the Inner Temple (a lawyer more interested in literature and the theatre than law); Sir Andrew Freeport, a merchant representing the rising commercial class and defending trade; Captain Sentry, an honest soldier; Will Honeycomb, an ageing man of fashion and ladies' man; and a clergyman of great learning and piety.

The aim of the Spectator was 'to enliven morality with wit, and to temper wit with morality'. Steele's sketches combine gentle humour with realistic characterisation and give a picture of 18th-century English society. They influenced the later development of the novel.
section-10: Other dramatic terms: exposition (introduction of characters and situation), rising action, falling action and denouement (final outcome), as in Freytag's pyramid. A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage reveals inner thoughts (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'); an aside is a short remark heard by the audience but not by other characters; a monologue is a long speech by one character.

From Aristotle's 'Poetics': catharsis is the purging of the emotions of pity and fear; hamartia is the tragic flaw or error of judgement of the hero; hubris is excessive pride; peripeteia is reversal of fortune; and anagnorisis is the moment of recognition.
section-11: Comedy types include romantic comedy (Shakespeare's 'As You Like It'), comedy of humours (Ben Jonson), comedy of manners (Congreve's 'The Way of the World'), farce and satirical comedy. Tragedy, according to Aristotle, is the imitation of a serious, complete action of a certain magnitude that arouses pity and fear and achieves catharsis. Examples: Sophocles' 'Oedipus Rex', Shakespeare's 'Hamlet', 'Macbeth', 'Othello' and 'King Lear'.

Tragicomedy mixes tragic and comic elements, usually with a serious plot that ends happily, e.g. Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' and 'The Merchant of Venice'. Modern examples include Beckett's 'Waiting for Godot', called a 'tragicomedy in two acts'.
section-12: 'Everyman' is a late 15th-century English morality play (possibly from the Dutch 'Elckerlijc'). Morality plays used allegorical characters to teach moral and religious lessons. God sends Death to summon Everyman to give an account of his life. Everyman asks Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin and Goods to accompany him, but all refuse. Good Deeds is too weak because of his sins; she introduces him to Knowledge, who leads him to Confession, where he does penance.

Then Beauty, Strength, Discretion and Five Wits join him but abandon him at the grave. Only Good Deeds goes with him to the end. The play teaches that worldly possessions and relationships cannot save a person; only good deeds, repentance and God's grace matter. Characters are personifications (allegory), and the language is simple and direct.
section-13: Characterisation can be direct (the narrator tells us about the character) or indirect (through actions, speech and thoughts). E.M. Forster distinguished flat characters (simple, built around one idea) and round characters (complex, capable of surprising). The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist opposes him.

Point of view may be first-person (narrator is a character, 'I'), third-person limited, third-person omniscient (all-knowing narrator) or second-person. Foreshadowing hints at future events. Irony may be verbal, situational or dramatic. Setting is the time and place of the story. A symbol is an object or event with deeper meaning.
section-14: Published in 1945, the novel is an allegory of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the rise of Stalin. Old Major (Lenin/Marx) inspires the animals with a dream of freedom; after his death, the animals of Manor Farm, led by the pigs Snowball (Trotsky) and Napoleon (Stalin), overthrow the farmer Mr. Jones (the Tsar) and rename it Animal Farm. They adopt the Seven Commandments, summarised as 'Four legs good, two legs bad'.

Napoleon uses his dogs (secret police) to expel Snowball, and Squealer (propaganda) twists the truth. Boxer, the hard-working horse ('I will work harder'), represents the loyal working class and is finally sold to the knacker. The commandments are secretly changed until only one remains: 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.' In the end, the pigs walk on two legs and become indistinguishable from humans. Themes: corruption of power, propaganda, betrayal of revolutionary ideals and totalitarianism.
section-16: Poetic devices and forms: Figures of speech such as simile, metaphor, personification, apostrophe, hyperbole, oxymoron and paradox add depth; sound devices such as alliteration, assonance, rhyme and onomatopoeia create music; imagery and symbolism appeal to the senses and suggest wider meanings. Forms include the ballad, epic, elegy, lyric, ode and sonnet. Structures include blank verse, free verse, couplets, quatrains and various metres.

La Belle Dame Sans Merci - summary: A speaker meets a pale, lonely knight in a desolate landscape in late autumn. The knight explains that he met a beautiful fairy lady, fell in love, and was taken to her elfin grot, where he dreamed of pale kings and warriors who warned that the lady had enslaved them too. He awoke alone on the cold hill side, still haunted.

Themes and techniques: The poem explores the fatal attraction of beauty, the dangers of romantic obsession, the conflict between dream and reality, and the sense of loss and desolation. It uses the ballad form with a question-and-answer structure, a shortened last line in each stanza, medieval setting, supernatural elements, symbolism (withered sedge, silent birds) and a circular ending.

Critical note: Some critics read the lady as a symbol of the poet's muse, of love, or even of death and disease (Keats was suffering and in love with Fanny Brawne). The poem is one of the best examples of the Romantic revival of the ballad.
section-17: Prose devices: Diction, tone, antithesis, figurative language, rhetoric and satire shape the effect of prose. The essay is a flexible form - periodical, personal, formal or argumentative - used by Bacon, Addison, Steele, Lamb and others.

The Spectator Club - background: Steele and Addison's 'The Spectator' (1711-12) was a daily periodical that aimed to improve manners and morals in an entertaining way. In No. 2, Steele introduces the members of the club that supposedly produced the paper.

Characters: Sir Roger de Coverley (a good-natured country squire, eccentric but kind), the Templar (a lawyer devoted to literature and the stage), Sir Andrew Freeport (a successful, sensible merchant who praises trade), Captain Sentry (a modest, brave soldier), Will Honeycomb (an ageing fashionable gentleman) and a learned, devout clergyman. Together they represent the landed gentry, law, commerce, army, fashionable society and the church.

Significance: The sketches combine humour, gentle satire and realism, reflect the social life of early 18th-century England and mark an important stage in the development of the English essay and character writing, preparing the way for the novel.
section-18: Drama terms: Drama is divided into acts and scenes and follows a plot structure of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Soliloquy and aside reveal inner thoughts. Aristotle's concepts of catharsis, hamartia, hubris, peripeteia and anagnorisis explain tragedy.

Forms: Comedy deals with human follies and ends happily (romantic comedy, comedy of manners, farce); tragedy presents the fall of a noble hero through a flaw and evokes pity and fear; tragicomedy mixes both.

Everyman - summary and allegory: God sends Death to summon Everyman. Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin and Goods desert him; Good Deeds, weakened by his sins, is revived through Knowledge and Confession. Beauty, Strength, Discretion and Five Wits accompany him but leave at the grave; only Good Deeds goes with him to judgement, and an Angel receives his soul.

Themes and significance: The play teaches the transience of worldly things, the importance of good deeds, repentance and divine grace. It is the best-known English morality play, using personified abstractions, simple verse and a clear moral message, and it links medieval religious drama with the later development of English drama.
section-19: Fiction terms: Novel, novella and short story differ in length and complexity. Elements of fiction include plot, conflict (man vs man, nature, society, self), characterisation (flat and round characters), setting, point of view, foreshadowing, irony and symbolism.

Animal Farm - plot: Inspired by Old Major's dream, the animals rebel against Mr. Jones. The pigs take leadership; Snowball and Napoleon quarrel over the windmill; Napoleon expels Snowball with his dogs and becomes a dictator. Squealer's propaganda justifies every abuse, the commandments are altered, Boxer is betrayed, and the pigs finally become like the humans they replaced.

Allegory: Old Major represents Marx/Lenin, Napoleon Stalin, Snowball Trotsky, Squealer the propaganda machine, the dogs the secret police, Boxer the working class, Moses the raven organised religion, and Mr. Jones the Tsar. The windmill stands for Stalin's Five-Year Plans.

Themes and style: The novel shows how revolutions can be betrayed, how power corrupts, how language is manipulated for control, and how ignorance and blind loyalty allow tyranny. Orwell called it a 'fairy story', and its simple style and animal characters make its political satire powerful and universal.
section-22: The Elizabethan Age (1558-1603) takes its name from Queen Elizabeth I. It was a time of national pride after the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588), voyages of discovery, the Reformation and the influence of the Italian Renaissance.

Major writers: Edmund Spenser ('The Faerie Queene', 'The Shepheardes Calendar'), Sir Philip Sidney ('Astrophel and Stella', 'An Apology for Poetry'), Christopher Marlowe ('Doctor Faustus'), William Shakespeare (plays and sonnets), the University Wits and Francis Bacon (essays). Features include the sonnet sequence, blank verse drama, pastoral poetry and a rich, experimental use of language.
section-23: The Restoration (1660-1700) began when Charles II returned from exile in France, ending the Puritan Commonwealth. Theatres, which had been closed by the Puritans in 1642, were reopened, and actresses appeared on stage for the first time.

Major writers include John Dryden (poet laureate, 'Absalom and Achitophel', 'MacFlecknoe'), John Milton ('Paradise Lost', 1667), John Bunyan ('The Pilgrim's Progress'), Samuel Butler ('Hudibras'), and dramatists William Wycherley and William Congreve. Features include heroic couplets, satire, the comedy of manners, scientific spirit (Royal Society, 1660) and French influence.
section-24: The 18th century is often called the Neo-classical Age or the Age of Reason, including the Augustan Age (Pope, Swift, Addison, Steele) and the Age of Johnson. Writers valued order, reason, decorum, wit and imitation of classical models.

Major developments: the periodical essay (The Tatler, The Spectator), satire (Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock', Swift's 'Gulliver's Travels'), Dr. Johnson's 'Dictionary' (1755), and the rise of the novel - Defoe ('Robinson Crusoe', 'Moll Flanders'), Richardson ('Pamela'), Fielding ('Tom Jones') and Sterne. Later in the century, pre-Romantic poets like Gray and Burns appeared.
section-25: Published in 1579, 'The Shepheardes Calendar' was Spenser's first major work, dedicated to Sir Philip Sidney. It contains twelve eclogues, one for each month from January to December, with woodcut illustrations and commentary by 'E.K.'. Its main character is the shepherd Colin Clout, who represents Spenser himself and suffers from unrequited love for Rosalind.

Eclogues are of three types: plaintive (complaints of love, e.g. January and December), recreative (songs and contests, e.g. April with its praise of Queen Elizabeth as 'Eliza') and moral (discussions of religion and the church, e.g. May, July and September). Spenser used archaic language and varied metres. The work marked the beginning of the English literary Renaissance.
section-26: Restoration comedy, also called the comedy of manners, flourished from 1660 to about 1710. Major dramatists include George Etherege ('The Man of Mode'), William Wycherley ('The Country Wife'), William Congreve ('Love for Love', 'The Way of the World'), Vanbrugh and Farquhar.

Features: witty dialogue and repartee, intrigue and complicated plots, characters from fashionable London society (fops, wits, rakes, jealous husbands, coquettes), themes of love, marriage, money and reputation, and a cynical view of morality. Jeremy Collier attacked its immorality in 1698, leading to a decline and the rise of sentimental comedy.
section-27: 'The Way of the World' (1700) is considered the finest comedy of manners. Mirabell, a witty gentleman, loves Millamant, a brilliant and independent young lady. However, Millamant's aunt, Lady Wishfort, controls half of her fortune and hates Mirabell because he once pretended to court her. Mirabell plots to trick Lady Wishfort by disguising his servant Waitwell as 'Sir Rowland'.

The villains Fainall and Mrs. Marwood discover the plot and try to blackmail Lady Wishfort to gain control of her daughter Mrs. Fainall's fortune. Mirabell defeats them by producing a deed through which Mrs. Fainall had earlier transferred her property to him in trust. The famous 'proviso scene' (Act IV), in which Mirabell and Millamant set conditions for their marriage, shows a relationship based on mutual respect and equality. The play satirises greed, hypocrisy and fashionable society.
section-28: Published in 1722, 'Moll Flanders' is a first-person picaresque novel. Moll was born in Newgate prison to a convicted mother. She is raised in a gentle family, seduced by the elder son and marries the younger. After several marriages - including one in Virginia where she discovers that her husband is her half-brother - she becomes poor and turns to theft, becoming one of the most skilful thieves in London.

She is finally caught and imprisoned in Newgate, where she repents. Her sentence of death is changed to transportation to America, where she and her Lancashire husband (Jemy) prosper as planters. Themes: the power of money, survival of a woman in a male-dominated society, crime and repentance, and individualism. Defoe's realistic details and plain style make it an important early English novel.
section-30: Elizabethan Age (1558-1603): The English Renaissance brought renewed interest in classical learning, exploration and national confidence after the defeat of the Spanish Armada. Poetry flourished with Spenser, Sidney and the sonnet sequences; drama reached great heights with Marlowe, the University Wits and Shakespeare, who used blank verse powerfully. Prose developed through Bacon's essays and Sidney's criticism.

Restoration Period (1660-1700): With the return of Charles II, theatres reopened and literature became witty, satirical and urban. Dryden dominated poetry and criticism, using the heroic couplet for satire; Milton's 'Paradise Lost' and Bunyan's 'Pilgrim's Progress' represented the Puritan spirit; Restoration comedy of manners by Etherege, Wycherley and Congreve satirised fashionable society.

Eighteenth Century: The Age of Reason valued order, decorum and classical rules. The periodical essays of Addison and Steele, the satires of Pope and Swift and the scholarship of Dr. Johnson shaped prose and poetry. The novel emerged with Defoe, Richardson, Fielding and Sterne, reflecting the rise of the middle class and interest in realistic life.
Conclusion: These periods show the movement of English literature from Renaissance imagination, through Restoration wit, to Augustan reason and the birth of the modern novel.
section-31: Background: Published in 1579, 'The Shepheardes Calendar' introduced Spenser as a major poet and is considered the starting point of the Elizabethan literary renaissance. It follows the pastoral tradition of Theocritus, Virgil and Mantuan and is dedicated to Sir Philip Sidney.

Structure: Twelve eclogues correspond to the twelve months, tracing the life of Colin Clout from youth (spring) to age (winter). Each eclogue has a woodcut, an argument, a dialogue or song, an emblem and E.K.'s glosses.

Themes: Plaintive eclogues deal with Colin's unrequited love for Rosalind; recreative eclogues include singing contests and the April eclogue praising Queen Elizabeth as Eliza, queen of shepherds; moral eclogues discuss corruption in the church, the role of poetry and the duties of pastors.

Style and significance: Spenser experimented with metres and used archaic and rustic words to create an English poetic language. The work combined pastoral convention with contemporary religious and political comment and established Spenser's reputation as 'the poet's poet'.
section-32: Plot: Mirabell loves Millamant, but she will lose half her fortune if she marries without the consent of her aunt, Lady Wishfort, who hates Mirabell. Mirabell has his servant Waitwell marry Foible (Lady Wishfort's maid) and disguise himself as Sir Rowland to court Lady Wishfort, intending to use the scandal to gain her consent. Fainall and his mistress Mrs. Marwood expose the plot and attempt to blackmail Lady Wishfort. Mirabell triumphs by revealing a deed of trust signed by Mrs. Fainall, protecting her fortune, and he wins Millamant.

Characters: Mirabell (witty, clever lover), Millamant (witty, independent heroine), Lady Wishfort (vain, ageing widow), Fainall (villainous, mercenary husband), Mrs. Marwood (jealous, scheming), Witwoud and Petulant (fops), and Sir Wilfull Witwoud (a country squire).

Themes: Love and marriage, money and inheritance, reputation, deception and the 'way of the world', i.e. the selfish and calculating behaviour of fashionable society. The proviso scene presents a modern idea of marriage based on mutual respect and freedom.
Style: Brilliant witty dialogue, complex plotting and satire make it the finest comedy of manners, though its complicated plot made it less popular on its first performance.
section-33: Plot: Born in Newgate, Moll grows up as a servant in a respectable family, is seduced by the elder brother and marries the younger. After his death she marries several times - including a draper, and a man in Virginia who turns out to be her half-brother - and has many children. Growing poor and older, she becomes a skilled thief in London, is finally arrested, repents in Newgate and is transported to Virginia with her husband Jemy, where they become prosperous.

Character of Moll: She is resourceful, practical, determined and calculating, but also capable of affection and repentance. Her life shows how poverty and the limited options for women pushed them into dependence on marriage or crime.
Themes: Money and economic survival, the position of women, crime and punishment, repentance and salvation (Puritan spiritual autobiography), and individualism in an emerging capitalist society.

Style and significance: Written as a first-person confession in plain, realistic prose with detailed accounts of money and objects, it is an important early English novel and a picaresque narrative that influenced later realistic fiction.
section-36: Examples of simile: 'My love is like a red, red rose' (Burns); 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' (Wordsworth). Examples of metaphor: 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare); 'Life is but a walking shadow'.

A simile makes the comparison explicit and is softer; a metaphor identifies one thing with another and is stronger. An extended metaphor continues across several lines, and a mixed metaphor combines unrelated images. Both help make abstract ideas vivid and concrete.
section-37: Allusions may be biblical, mythological, historical or literary. Example: 'He was a Judas' (betrayal); in Eliot's 'Journey of the Magi', 'three trees on the low sky' alludes to the crucifixion. Allusions enrich meaning but require shared knowledge between poet and reader.

Personification examples: 'Death, be not proud' (Donne); 'Because I could not stop for Death - / He kindly stopped for me' (Dickinson); Keats's autumn 'sitting careless on a granary floor'. It makes abstract ideas and nature lively and emotionally close to the reader.
section-38: Alliteration examples: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers'; 'The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew' (Coleridge). It creates rhythm, emphasis and musical effect and makes lines memorable.

Climax in rhetoric arranges words or ideas in increasing order of importance: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (Caesar). The opposite is anticlimax or bathos, a sudden fall from the serious to the trivial, as in Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock'. In plot, the climax is the turning point of highest tension.
section-39: Lyric: originally a song sung to the lyre, a lyric is short, personal, emotional and musical; it includes sonnets, odes, elegies and songs. Sonnet: the Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet has an octave (abbaabba) and sestet (cdecde or cdcdcd) with a turn (volta); the Shakespearean (English) sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet (abab cdcd efef gg); the Spenserian sonnet uses interlocking rhyme (abab bcbc cdcd ee).

Ode: the Pindaric ode has strophe, antistrophe and epode; the Horatian ode has regular stanzas; the irregular ode varies freely. Keats's great odes of 1819 ('Ode to a Nightingale', 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', 'To Autumn') are famous examples.
section-40: The term 'metaphysical' was used by Dr. Johnson in his 'Life of Cowley' to describe 17th-century poets like John Donne, George Herbert, Andrew Marvell, Henry Vaughan and Richard Crashaw. T.S. Eliot later praised their 'unified sensibility'.

Features: the metaphysical conceit (far-fetched comparison, such as Donne's comparison of lovers to the legs of a compass in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning'), wit, argumentative structure, colloquial and dramatic openings ('Busy old fool, unruly sun'), use of learning from science, theology and philosophy, and themes of love, religion and death.
section-41: Features: a single speaker who is not the poet, a silent listener whose presence is felt, a specific dramatic situation, and the gradual revelation of the speaker's character, often unintentionally. Robert Browning perfected it in 'My Last Duchess', where the Duke reveals his jealousy and cruelty while showing a portrait of his late wife.
Other examples include Tennyson's 'Ulysses' and T.S. Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'. It combines lyric and dramatic qualities and allows psychological depth.
section-42: Sonnet 130 begins: 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red than her lips' red'. The speaker says that her breasts are 'dun' rather than white like snow, her hair is like 'black wires', there are no roses in her cheeks, her breath 'reeks' compared to perfume, her voice is less pleasing than music and she 'treads on the ground' instead of walking like a goddess.

The final couplet - 'And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare / As any she belied with false compare' - shows that his love is genuine and does not need false comparisons. The sonnet parodies the Petrarchan conventions of idealised beauty and celebrates realistic, sincere love. It follows the Shakespearean form (abab cdcd efef gg) in iambic pentameter.
section-43: 'To Autumn' (1819) has three eleven-line stanzas. Stanza 1 describes autumn as the 'season of mists and mellow fruitfulness', a friend of the sun, loading vines with fruit, swelling the gourd and filling the honeycombs. Stanza 2 personifies autumn as a harvester sitting 'careless on a granary floor', asleep in a half-reaped furrow, a gleaner, and watching the cider-press. Stanza 3 asks 'Where are the songs of Spring?' and answers that autumn has its own music - gnats, lambs, crickets, the robin and 'gathering swallows'.

The poem moves from morning to evening and from ripeness to the approach of winter. It accepts the natural cycle of growth and decline. It is rich in sensuous imagery (sight, touch, taste, sound) and is considered one of the most perfect poems in English.
section-44: 'Death, be not proud' is Holy Sonnet X by John Donne, written in Petrarchan form with a Shakespearean-style couplet. The speaker uses apostrophe and personification to address Death and argues that Death is not 'mighty and dreadful'.

Arguments: rest and sleep, which are images of death, give pleasure, so death must give more; the best men go with Death to find rest; Death is a 'slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men' and lives with 'poison, war, and sickness'; poppies and charms can make us sleep as well. The final line - 'And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die' - presents the Christian belief in resurrection and eternal life. It is a fine example of metaphysical wit and paradox.
section-45: Published in 1927, soon after Eliot joined the Anglican Church, the poem is a dramatic monologue spoken by one of the Magi (wise men) in old age. It opens with words adapted from Lancelot Andrewes' sermon: 'A cold coming we had of it'. The journey was difficult - bad weather, rebellious camel men, hostile cities and unfriendly villages - and they were tempted by memories of 'summer palaces' and 'silken girls'.

Symbols foreshadow the crucifixion: 'three trees on the low sky', 'six hands at an open door dicing for pieces of silver', 'a white horse'. They found the birth 'satisfactory', but it was 'hard and bitter agony for us, like Death, our death'. After returning, they were 'no longer at ease here, in the old dispensation'. The poem shows that spiritual rebirth involves the death of the old self.
section-46: Nissim Ezekiel (1924-2004) was a pioneer of modern Indian poetry in English. In the poem, the speaker remembers the night his mother was stung by a scorpion during heavy rain. The villagers come 'like swarms of flies', buzz the name of God, search for the scorpion with candles and lanterns, and say that each movement of the scorpion's poison would burn away sins of a previous birth.

The father, a sceptic and rationalist, tries 'every curse and blessing, powder, mixture, herb and hybrid' and even pours paraffin on the bitten toe; a holy man performs rites. After twenty hours the poison loses its sting. The mother's final words - 'Thank God the scorpion picked on me and spared my children' - show selfless maternal love. Themes: superstition versus science, community life, and a mother's love. The poem uses free verse, irony and vivid imagery.
section-47: Emily Dickinson (1830-1886), an American poet, wrote this poem around 1863. Death is personified as a polite gentleman caller who 'kindly stopped' for the speaker in a carriage, accompanied by Immortality. They drive slowly past a school where children play (childhood), fields of gazing grain (maturity) and the setting sun (old age and death).

The speaker feels the chill of the dews, dressed only in a gossamer gown, and they pause at a house that seems 'a swelling of the ground' (the grave). The last stanza reveals that centuries have passed, yet it feels shorter than the day she first guessed the horses' heads were 'toward Eternity'. Features: dashes, slant rhyme, common metre (alternating tetrameter and trimeter), calm tone and themes of death, immortality and the journey of life.
section-49: Figures of speech: Simile and metaphor create comparisons; allusion enriches meaning through references to known stories; personification gives life to abstract ideas and nature; alliteration creates musical effect; climax arranges ideas in increasing intensity. Other devices include imagery, symbolism, hyperbole, paradox and apostrophe.

Lyric, sonnet and ode: The lyric expresses personal emotion; the sonnet is a fourteen-line form in Petrarchan, Shakespearean and Spenserian varieties; the ode is a serious, elaborate lyric often addressed to a person or object, in Pindaric, Horatian or irregular forms.
Metaphysical poetry: Donne and his followers used conceits, wit, argument, colloquial language and learned imagery to explore love and religion, uniting thought and feeling.

Dramatic monologue: Developed by Browning and used by Tennyson and Eliot, it presents a single speaker addressing a silent listener and reveals character and situation. Understanding these devices and forms helps students analyse prescribed poems and write strong critical answers.
section-50: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130: It is an anti-Petrarchan sonnet that rejects conventional exaggerations of beauty - eyes like the sun, lips like coral, cheeks like roses - and describes the mistress realistically. The couplet asserts that his love is as rare as any woman praised with false comparisons, celebrating sincere love over flattery.

Keats's 'To Autumn': Through three stanzas, Keats presents autumn's ripeness, its personification as a harvester and gleaner, and its own music in the evening. The poem progresses from abundance to quiet decline, accepting the cycle of life and death, and is rich in sensuous imagery.

Donne's 'Death, be not proud': Addressing Death directly, Donne argues logically that Death is not powerful but a slave to fate and chance, merely a short sleep before eternal life. The paradoxical conclusion, 'Death, thou shalt die', expresses Christian faith in resurrection.

Comparison: Shakespeare uses wit to redefine love, Keats uses imagery to celebrate nature and transience, and Donne uses argument to defeat death. All three show mastery of form - the sonnet and the ode - and deal with universal themes of beauty, time and mortality.
section-51: Eliot's 'Journey of the Magi': A dramatic monologue by one of the wise men recalling the hard journey to Bethlehem, the symbolic images foreshadowing the crucifixion, and the feeling that the birth was also a death of their old way of life. It explores spiritual conversion and alienation.

Ezekiel's 'Night of the Scorpion': The poet remembers his mother's suffering after a scorpion sting, the villagers' superstitious prayers and theories about karma, the father's rationalism mixed with desperation, and the mother's selfless words at the end. It contrasts superstition and reason and celebrates maternal love, in an Indian setting with ironic detachment.

Dickinson's 'Because I Could Not Stop for Death': Death, a courteous gentleman, takes the speaker on a carriage ride past scenes representing the stages of life to the grave and towards eternity. The calm tone, personification and dashes express her unique view of death as a passage rather than an end.

Comparison: Each poem presents a journey - spiritual (Eliot), domestic and emotional (Ezekiel) and from life to eternity (Dickinson) - and uses a personal or dramatic voice to reflect on faith, suffering and mortality across British, Indian and American contexts.
section-54: The word 'communication' comes from the Latin 'communicare', meaning 'to share' or 'to make common'. Communication may be intrapersonal (with oneself), interpersonal (between two people), group, public and mass communication.

Its purposes include informing, persuading, instructing, entertaining and building relationships. Communication is a two-way process; it is complete only when the receiver understands the message as intended.
section-55: Steps: (1) the sender has an idea; (2) the sender encodes it into words, symbols or gestures; (3) the message is transmitted through a channel (speech, letter, email, phone); (4) the receiver receives it; (5) the receiver decodes or interprets it; (6) the receiver responds with feedback.

Models include Aristotle's model (speaker, speech, audience), Shannon and Weaver's model (including noise) and Berlo's SMCR model (source, message, channel, receiver). Noise at any stage can distort the message.
section-56: Sender: the person who initiates communication. Message: the information, idea or feeling being shared. Channel or medium: the means used, such as speech, writing, telephone, email or social media. Receiver: the person or audience for whom the message is meant. Feedback: the response that shows whether the message was understood.

Context: the physical setting, social relationship, cultural background and time in which communication happens. Noise: any disturbance (physical, psychological or semantic) that interferes with communication.
section-57: Factors include: the sender's knowledge, attitude and communication skills; clarity and organisation of the message; choice of an appropriate channel; the receiver's attention, background and attitude; language and vocabulary; cultural norms; emotions; the relationship between sender and receiver; and the physical environment such as noise and seating.
Considering the purpose and audience helps the speaker or writer choose suitable tone, language and medium.
section-58: Oral communication includes face-to-face conversations, telephone calls, meetings, lectures, interviews and presentations. It is quick, allows immediate feedback and expresses emotion through tone, but it may be forgotten and is not easily recorded.

Written communication includes letters, emails, reports, notices, memos and essays. It provides a permanent record, allows careful planning and can reach many people, but it takes time and feedback is delayed. Good verbal communication follows the 7 Cs: clarity, conciseness, concreteness, correctness, consideration, completeness and courtesy.
section-59: Types of non-verbal communication: kinesics (body movements, gestures, posture, facial expressions), oculesics (eye contact), proxemics (use of space and distance), haptics (touch), chronemics (use of time), paralanguage (tone, pitch, pace, pauses) and appearance (dress, grooming). Albert Mehrabian's research suggests that much of the emotional meaning of a message comes from tone and body language.
Non-verbal cues may reinforce, contradict, substitute or regulate verbal messages. They vary across cultures, so awareness is important in intercultural communication.
section-60: Types of barriers: physical barriers (noise, distance, poor network); semantic barriers (jargon, ambiguous words, different meanings); psychological barriers (emotions, prejudice, lack of attention, fear); cultural barriers (different customs, values and gestures); organisational barriers (hierarchy, rigid rules); and personal barriers (poor listening, lack of confidence).
Barriers cause misunderstanding, conflict and loss of time and efficiency.
section-61: Strategies: use simple, clear and precise language; know the audience; choose the right medium; organise ideas logically; listen actively (pay attention, avoid interrupting, ask questions, paraphrase); seek and give feedback; control emotions; be sensitive to cultural differences; use non-verbal cues consistently; and reduce physical noise.
Following the 7 Cs of communication and practising empathy also help overcome barriers.
section-62: Elements of voice: pronunciation and articulation (speaking words clearly and correctly); pitch (high or low); volume (loudness appropriate to the audience and room); pace or rate (not too fast or too slow); tone (friendly, formal, enthusiastic); stress and intonation (emphasising key words and using rising and falling patterns); and pauses (to emphasise points and allow understanding).
Practice methods include reading aloud, recording one's voice, breathing exercises, tongue twisters and speaking in front of a mirror or friends.
section-63: Preparation for an interview: research the organisation, understand the job requirements, prepare answers to common questions (e.g. 'Tell me about yourself', strengths and weaknesses, why you want the job), prepare documents, dress formally and arrive on time.

During the interview: greet politely, maintain eye contact and good posture, listen carefully, answer clearly and honestly, give examples, avoid negative comments, ask relevant questions at the end and thank the panel. A mock interview simulates this experience, and feedback helps improve body language, content and confidence.
section-64: A seminar usually involves a presenter who prepares a paper or talk on a topic, followed by questions and discussion moderated by a chairperson. It develops research, critical thinking, speaking and listening skills.

Steps: choose and research the topic, prepare an outline (introduction, main points, conclusion), prepare notes or slides, rehearse, present within the time limit, and respond to questions politely and confidently. Participants should listen attentively and contribute constructively.
section-65: Structure: introduction (greeting, topic, purpose, overview), body (main points with examples, data and visuals) and conclusion (summary, key message, invitation for questions).

Tips: know the audience, keep slides simple (few words, clear images), maintain eye contact, use appropriate voice and gestures, manage time, avoid reading from slides, handle questions calmly and practise in advance. Visual aids such as PowerPoint, charts and videos should support, not replace, the speaker.
section-67: Meaning: Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas and feelings to create shared meaning. It may be intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public or mass communication.

Process: The sender conceives an idea, encodes it into a message, sends it through a channel, the receiver decodes it and gives feedback. Models such as Shannon-Weaver and Berlo's SMCR explain this process and the effect of noise.
Elements: Sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context and noise are the main elements. Each must function well for effective communication.

Factors: The sender's skills and attitudes, clarity of the message, choice of channel, the receiver's background and attention, language, culture, emotions, relationships and environment influence communication. Effective communicators consider purpose and audience and check understanding through feedback.
section-68: Verbal communication: Oral communication (conversations, speeches, meetings, phone calls) is fast and allows immediate feedback; written communication (letters, emails, reports) provides a permanent record and allows careful expression. The 7 Cs guide effective verbal communication.
Non-verbal communication: Body language, facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, posture, space, touch, time and paralanguage convey attitudes and emotions and can reinforce or contradict words.
Barriers: Physical, semantic, psychological, cultural, organisational and personal barriers distort messages and cause misunderstanding.

Overcoming barriers: Using simple language, knowing the audience, choosing suitable channels, active listening, feedback, emotional control, cultural sensitivity and consistent non-verbal signals make communication effective.
section-69: Vocal techniques: Clear pronunciation, varied pitch and intonation, appropriate volume and pace, meaningful pauses and a suitable tone make speech pleasant and persuasive.

Mock interviews: Practising interviews helps students prepare answers, improve body language, manage anxiety and present themselves professionally. Preparation, punctuality, formal dress, eye contact, honest answers and polite behaviour are essential.
Seminars: A seminar requires research on a topic, an organised paper or talk, confident presentation and constructive discussion. It develops academic and critical skills.

Presentations: A good presentation has a clear structure (introduction, body, conclusion), simple visual aids, eye contact, good voice control, time management and the ability to handle questions. Regular practice builds the confidence needed for academic and professional success.
